vignette:
He sits in the chair across from me, hands folded loosely on his knees, eyes fixed on a spot where the carpet meets the wall. He is a doctor—has been for forty-three years—and even now, in this room, there is a careful stillness to him, a professional composure that cracks only when he speaks about his daughter.

The story starts twenty years ago. He was forty-seven, a cardiologist in a busy practice, raising his only child alone after his wife left when the girl was three. He tells me she was bright, stubborn, a painter. She was fifteen when she started losing weight, complaining of bone pain. He recognized the signs before the tests came back—osteosarcoma in her left femur. He remembers the moment of diagnosis not as a shock but as a terrible clarity, a piece of knowledge he could not put back.

They began treatment. He threw himself into the role of father-physician, attending every oncology consult, reviewing every scan, questioning every protocol. He told himself that his medical knowledge would save her. But knowledge did not protect him from the waiting, the vomiting after chemo, the night she seized from febrile neutropenia and he had to stand aside while the ICU team worked. He remembers standing in the hospital corridor, his white coat still on, feeling utterly useless.

She survived. The cancer went into remission after a year of treatment. She is now thirty-five, living in another state, healthy. He should be relieved. Instead, he describes a quiet dread that has never left. For years he has woken at three in the morning to check his phone for missed calls, certain that something is wrong. He avoids the oncology wing of his hospital entirely, taking longer routes through the basement to get to his office. When a patient mentions a child’s illness, he changes the subject or finds a reason to leave the room.

The PCL-5 score of fifty-four is only a number. In session, I see the symptoms in the way he startles when I shift in my chair. He tells me he cannot watch medical dramas, cannot read articles about adolescent cancers, cannot go to the pediatric floor to see a colleague’s child after an appendectomy. He has stopped attending family gatherings because his daughter’s cousins have young children now, and one of them might cough, and he will start to imagine the worst.

He still works part-time, but his caseload is limited to older adults with stable conditions. He is meticulous, perhaps overly so—ordering extra tests, keeping patients longer than necessary. He cannot stand uncertainty. He says, “I know the statistics. I know she’s fine. But my body doesn’t know.” When I ask him what his body feels, he describes a constant low-level tightness in his chest, a humming alertness that never shuts off. He has not had a full night’s sleep since her diagnosis.

He is single, has been since the divorce. He tells me there was a woman he dated a few years after his daughter’s recovery, but he ended it when she mentioned wanting children. The thought of going through that fear again was unbearable. He says, “I think I used all my worry up. I don’t have any left for anyone else.”

He comes to therapy because his daughter recently told him she is thinking about having a child of her own. The news has triggered a resurgence of nightmares—vivid scenes of her in a hospital bed, his hands shaking as he tries to read a monitor. During the day, he finds himself driving past the hospital where she was treated, circling the block, unable to leave.

He does not cry when he tells me these things. He is a doctor, after all. But I notice that his hands have tightened into fists, and when I look at his face, I see the same expression he must have worn twenty years ago: a man trying to hold on, even as the ground falls away.
